newsitem.title: EGYPT: PLO rings alarm, Israel positive on talks.
newsitem.headline: PLO rings alarm, Israel positive on talks.

text.p: The PLO rang alarm bells but Israel sounded a positive note on negotiations to implement a long-delayed Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.
Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and Israeli negotiators resumed formal talks late on Wednesday night at the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba.
The sides huddled with mediator U.S. envoy Dennis Ross to thrash out a work plan for the negotiations.

"We decided that the security and civilian committees will meet together tonight and then a meeting of the leadership of the steering committee will start tomorrow to finalise the agenda," Palestinian negotiator Jamil Tarifi told Reuters.
Earlier on Wednesday in Cairo, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was enraged by an Israeli troop redeployment proposal presented on Tuesday night, describing it as a tragedy.
"It's a dangerous operation. It shows Israel's aggressive intentions in Hebron and shows complete and abhorrent racism," he told reporters in Cairo.
Arafat said the plan would, among other things, divide the West Bank town in two and give Israel the right to chase Arabs it wanted anywhere in Hebron, including in Palestinian-ruled areas.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said: "There is no plan to divide Hebron." Bazak refused to elaborate.
Netanyahu said without goodwill any issue could derail the talks.

"We are conducting the negotiations with goodwill. We hope we will encounter the same attitude from the other side," Netanyahu told Israel's army radio. "If there is an attitude like that, I have no doubt that we can finish it, even quickly.
"If there is not an attitude like that then each thing can be used as an excuse why we haven't finished."

"What's needed is for Mr Arafat to stop...travelling from place to place as if he has all the time in the world. And there is no room for these games because the subject is serious," Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told parliament.
"If he will show this responsibility, I believe that within a day we could close the subject in a deal," Levy said.
Palestinian negotiators said they complained to their Israeli counterparts about Levy's statement.

Palestinian team head Saeb Erekat said the PLO wanted to discuss not only the Hebron deal but implementation of all outstanding issues including further redeployments from rural West Bank areas, which, like Hebron, are part of a September 1995 accord expanding Palestinian West Bank self-rule.
"There is a lot of differences and there is a lot to be done," Ross told reporters.
Israeli team spokesman Moshe Fogel said the talks might have to go on until Friday morning.
The U.S.-sponsored talks are in their second week. The decision to hold them was taken at a Washington summit after clashes last month killed 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
The Hebron redeployment was set for March but was delayed by Israel after Islamic suicide attacks killed 59 people in Israel.
Netanyahu froze the deal, demanding that security be bolstered for 400 Jewish settlers living among 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron.

The Palestinians, backed by Israel's Arab neighbours, say security could be enhanced without altering the existing deal. They oppose any changes in the accord signed by Israel's previous government ousted by Netanyahu in May elections.
